TimeFocus.q: You are leading a project meeting with an international team. The agenda has 5 items, but the first topic sparks a rich, unexpected discussion. The scheduled time has passed. What do you do?
options: Politely interrupt and move to the next agenda item. The schedule must be respected.
Allow 2-3 extra minutes, then firmly redirect the group back to the agenda.
Quickly assess whether the discussion is more valuable than remaining items and adjust accordingly.
Let the discussion continue and drop the least important agenda item to compensate.
Fully embrace the organic flow. The best outcomes come from following the energy of the group.

TimeFocus.q: A colleague calls during your focused work time for a non-urgent matter. How do you respond?
options: I don't answer. I have blocked this time for deep work and will call back during open hours.
I answer briefly, explain I'm busy, and schedule a specific time to talk later.
I answer and spend a few minutes helping, then gently wrap up.
I take the call and help as long as needed. Relationships come first.
I'm happy to help. Interruptions are a natural part of the workday.

TimeFocus.q: You are organizing a social event for an international group. How do you structure the evening?
options: A detailed timeline: 7:00 arrivals, 7:30 dinner, 8:30 speeches, 9:30 networking, 10:30 close.
A loose framework with approximate start times but some flexibility built in.
A general plan (dinner, then socializing) but I let the evening unfold naturally.
Minimal structure. I provide food, drinks, and a space, and trust the group.
No schedule at all. People arrive when they arrive, eat when hungry, leave when ready.

TimeOrientation.q: Your organization is considering a major strategic change. What type of argument do you find most persuasive?
options: This approach has been tested for decades and has a proven track record.
This builds on established traditions while making careful, incremental improvements.
This respects our history but also positions us for emerging trends.
This is innovative and will give us a competitive advantage in the next 5 years.
This completely reimagines our model. We need to disrupt ourselves before someone else does.

TimeOrientation.q: A diplomatic delegation is visiting your city. What do you prioritize in the welcome program?
options: Historical monuments, museums, and sites showcasing our rich heritage.
A mix of historical sites and meetings with established institutions.
A balanced program honoring past achievements while showcasing current developments.
Tours of innovation hubs, tech parks, and startups showing where our country is heading.
Presentations on future megaprojects and emerging industries that don't exist yet.

TimeOrientation.q: When making an important personal decision (e.g., relocating), what weighs most heavily?
options: How this honors my family's history, roots, and previous generations' sacrifices.
Whether this is consistent with values and lessons from my past experiences.
A balance between honoring where I come from and creating new opportunities.
How this positions me for growth and success in the coming years.
The long-term vision of the life I want to build 10-20 years from now.

Space.q: You are working in a shared office with international colleagues. How do you feel about the workspace?
options: I need a closed door and clear boundaries. My workspace is my personal territory.
I prefer a quiet corner or partitioned desk with some visual and acoustic privacy.
I'm comfortable in open-plan if private meeting rooms are available when needed.
I enjoy open, shared spaces where I can interact with colleagues throughout the day.
I thrive in bustling, communal environments. The more people around, the more energized.

Space.q: A new colleague asks a personal question (salary, marital status) during work lunch. How do you react?
options: Very uncomfortable. This is private and has no place in a professional setting.
I give a vague, polite answer and steer back to work topics.
I share a little to be friendly but keep most details to myself.
I'm open to sharing. Knowing each other personally builds stronger professional trust.
I welcome it enthusiastically. There is no separation between personal and professional life.

Space.q: When hosting an international business dinner, how do you handle seating?
options: Assigned seats with clear place cards. Each person has their designated space.
Assigned seats for key guests, some flexibility for others.
General seating plan (this table for delegation, that for our team) but no specific seats.
Open seating. I encourage people to mix and sit wherever comfortable.
No seating plan. Everyone shares food family-style and moves around freely.

Power.q: During a negotiation, the most senior person on your team makes a statement with a factual error. What do you do?
options: I correct the error immediately and openly. Accuracy matters more than rank.
I raise my hand: 'If I may add a clarification...' in a respectful but direct tone.
I wait for a natural pause and gently reframe without explicitly calling it an error.
I say nothing during the meeting but send a private message afterward.
I would never contradict a senior leader in front of others. Their authority must be preserved.

Power.q: You are at a formal diplomatic reception. How do you approach greeting protocol?
options: I greet everyone equally with a handshake and first names, regardless of title.
I use titles for the most senior but am more casual with junior staff.
I follow my host's lead. If formal, I match; if casual, I match.
I research the hierarchy beforehand and greet the most senior person first with formalities.
I strictly observe all protocol: bowing, waiting to be introduced, full titles, deferring throughout.

Power.q: In a cross-cultural team project, how should decisions be made?
options: Every member has an equal vote regardless of position. The best idea wins.
Everyone shares opinions, but the team lead makes the final call.
The team discusses openly; the most experienced members naturally guide toward consensus.
The senior leader consults a small inner circle, then announces the decision.
The most senior person decides. Their authority makes them best suited to lead.

Structure.q: Your company offers you a prestigious individual award, but your team contributed significantly. How do you handle it?
options: I accept proudly. I earned it through individual effort and initiative.
I accept but publicly acknowledge my team's contributions in my speech.
I feel uncomfortable accepting alone and suggest sharing with the team.
I redirect recognition to the team. Group success matters more than individual achievement.
I decline the individual award and insist it go to the entire team.

Structure.q: You are assigned to a long-term project abroad. What is your primary relationship-building goal?
options: To expand my personal professional network and advance my individual career.
To build a few strong professional connections for mutual future benefit.
To integrate into the local community while maintaining independence and personal goals.
To become a trusted group member, prioritizing their needs alongside my own.
To fully immerse in the group's identity. My success is inseparable from the community's.

Structure.q: When facing a major life decision, whose opinion matters most?
options: My own. I trust my individual judgment above all else.
My own, but I value input from a close friend or mentor.
A balance between personal desires and family/close circle expectations.
My family and close community. Their well-being and approval are central.
The collective. I would not decide without full consensus from family and community.

Competition.q: In a business pitch competition, another team struggles with their technology. What do you do?
options: I focus on my own preparation. We are competitors; it's not my responsibility.
I wish them luck but don't intervene. Fair competition means managing your own challenges.
I offer a quick suggestion if I know the solution, but don't go out of my way.
I actively help them fix the issue. A good relationship matters more than winning.
I share my equipment freely. The best outcome is when everyone presents their best work.

Competition.q: Your company is setting performance targets. What approach do you advocate?
options: Individual targets with clear rankings and bonuses for top performers.
Individual targets with some team-based incentives to balance drive with collaboration.
A mix of individual and team goals with equal weight.
Team-based targets where the group succeeds or fails together.
Collective organizational goals only. Internal competition is destructive.

Competition.q: In a cross-cultural workshop, which group exercise format do you prefer?
options: A competitive debate where teams argue opposing positions and a winner is declared.
Structured exercise with scoring, but teams can learn from each other.
Collaborative problem-solving where all groups work on the same challenge and share results.
A cooperative simulation where all participants work together for a single shared outcome.
A community-building circle focused on mutual understanding, not producing a result.

Communication.q: You receive an email: 'Your proposal is interesting. We will think about it and get back to you when the time is right.' How do you interpret this?
options: They are genuinely interested and will contact me soon with specific feedback.
They are leaning positive but need more time. I'll follow up in a week.
I'm not sure. The message is ambiguous, so I'll wait and ask for clarification.
This is likely a polite refusal. 'Interesting' and 'when the time is right' suggest they won't say no directly.
This is clearly a 'no.' Direct rejection would be rude, so they signal refusal indirectly.

Communication.q: You need to give negative feedback to a colleague about their presentation. How do you deliver it?
options: Directly: 'Your presentation had three major issues. Here they are...'
Honestly but constructively: 'Good effort, but specific areas need improvement.'
Carefully, balancing positive and negative so the message is clear but not harsh.
Indirectly, by asking questions that guide them to identify issues themselves.
Very subtly, through hints or a trusted third party. Direct criticism would damage the relationship.

Communication.q: Your counterpart says 'yes' but their body language is hesitant. How do you proceed?
options: I take the 'yes' at face value and move forward with the agreement.
I note the hesitation but proceed, planning to confirm details in writing later.
I pause and ask: 'Are you comfortable with all aspects of this proposal?'
I read the non-verbal cues as discomfort and suggest revisiting with more flexibility.
The 'yes' is about harmony, not agreement. I slow down, rebuild rapport, and look for the real answer in what is NOT said.

Action.q: You meet a new international contact at a conference. What do you want to know first?
options: What do they do? Job title, company, current projects.
Their professional achievements and goals they're working toward.
A mix of what they do professionally and who they are as a person.
Where they're from, their family, what they enjoy outside work.
Who they are at their core—values, philosophy, what gives them meaning.

Action.q: Your organization evaluates a partnership's success. What metric matters most?
options: Tangible results: revenue, contracts signed, deadlines met.
Measurable outcomes combined with qualitative stakeholder feedback.
A balance between deliverables and relationship quality built during the process.
The depth of trust and mutual understanding established between partners.
The long-term harmony and shared purpose that emerged, regardless of short-term deliverables.

Action.q: When introducing yourself to international professionals, how do you describe yourself?
options: I'm a [title] at [company]. I specialize in [field] and recently completed [achievement].
I work in [field] and I'm passionate about [goal]. Currently focused on [project].
I work in [field], but I'm also a [hobby/identity]. I believe in balancing professional and personal growth.
I value deep connections and meaningful experiences. My relationships define me more than my title.
I'm a [cultural identity] who believes in [philosophy]. My work is just one expression of who I am.

PowerDistance.q: During a high-stakes negotiation, the most senior leader on your team makes a statement that contains a clear factual error. How do you respond?
options: I openly and immediately correct the error. Accuracy and truth are more important than rank.
I politely but directly interject to clarify the facts for the room.
I wait for a natural pause and gently suggest an alternative perspective without explicitly calling it an error.
I say nothing during the meeting, but send a private, polite message to the leader afterward.
I defer completely during the meeting and only discuss the discrepancy with a trusted peer later.
I accept the statement as is. In this setting, the leader's authority and the team's unified front override minor factual details.
I actively support the leader's statement to reinforce their authority, and I would only correct the record privately and very discreetly later if absolutely necessary.

PowerDistance.q: You are organizing a formal diplomatic reception. How do you handle the seating arrangement and greeting protocol?
options: Completely open seating and first-name greetings for everyone, regardless of title or age.
Mostly open seating, but I ensure the guest of honor gets a slightly better spot.
A general seating plan by delegation, with casual but respectful greetings.
Assigned seating for key figures, with a mix of formal and informal greetings based on familiarity.
Strictly assigned seating based on protocol, and I greet everyone using their formal titles.
Highly structured seating reflecting exact hierarchical rank, and I wait to be introduced before speaking to seniors.
Rigid protocol: seating is strictly by rank, and I use full formal titles, bowing or deferring appropriately, never speaking to a senior until addressed.

PowerDistance.q: Your team is facing a critical deadline. How should the final decision on the project direction be made?
options: A democratic vote where every team member, regardless of role, has an equal say.
An open discussion where the team lead considers all opinions but makes the final call.
The team discusses openly, and the most experienced members naturally guide the group to a consensus.
The team lead consults a small group of senior members, then announces the decision.
The senior leader makes the decision after brief input, and the team is expected to execute it without debate.
The most senior person decides entirely on their own. Their experience and authority make them best suited to lead.
The top leader dictates the direction. Questioning or debating this decision would be seen as insubordination and disrespect.

UncertaintyAvoidance.q: Your organization suddenly announces a major change in project scope with very little prior warning or detailed instruction. How do you react?
options: I embrace it immediately. Ambiguity is an exciting opportunity for innovation and creative problem-solving.
I am comfortable with it and will figure out the details as we go, adapting on the fly.
I am slightly uneasy but will ask a few clarifying questions and then proceed flexibly.
I feel a moderate need for clarity and will immediately draft a provisional plan to establish some structure.
I am quite uncomfortable and will actively seek out management to demand a detailed, step-by-step roadmap before proceeding.
I am highly anxious about the lack of rules. I will refuse to act until a comprehensive, formal procedure is written and approved.
I am deeply distressed by the ambiguity. I believe operating without strict, pre-approved protocols is reckless and unprofessional.

UncertaintyAvoidance.q: You are drafting a partnership agreement with a new international counterpart. What is your approach to the contract?
options: A brief, one-page memorandum of understanding. We trust each other and can adapt as needed.
A short agreement outlining the main goals, leaving the specific methods flexible.
A standard contract with clear objectives, but room for informal adjustments as the relationship evolves.
A detailed contract covering most foreseeable scenarios, with a formal process for amendments.
A highly detailed, lengthy contract with strict clauses, penalties, and explicit procedures for every possible contingency.
An exhaustive legal document. Every single rule, exception, and protocol must be explicitly defined to eliminate all risk.
A rigid, ironclad contract. Any deviation from the written rules without formal, multi-level approval is unacceptable.

UncertaintyAvoidance.q: A colleague proposes a completely new, untested method to solve a recurring problem. What is your immediate reaction?
options: I enthusiastically support it. We should always be experimenting and disrupting the status quo.
I am open to it and suggest we run a quick, low-risk pilot to see how it works.
I am cautiously optimistic but want to review the potential risks before committing.
I am hesitant and ask for a detailed risk assessment and a comparison with our current proven methods.
I am skeptical. I prefer we stick to the established procedures that we know work reliably.
I strongly oppose it. Introducing untested methods creates unnecessary and dangerous unpredictability.
I outright reject it. We must strictly adhere to our proven, standardized operating procedures without deviation.

InstitutionalCollectivism.q: Your company has a surplus budget at the end of the year. How do you believe it should be allocated?
options: Entirely as individual performance bonuses to reward the top-performing employees.
Mostly as individual bonuses, with a small portion for a team celebration.
A balanced split: half for individual merit bonuses, half for improving shared workplace resources.
Mostly toward improving shared resources and community programs, with modest individual bonuses.
Entirely toward collective benefits: upgrading shared facilities, funding team-wide training, or community initiatives.
Heavily into societal or organizational welfare programs, ensuring no individual stands out financially.
Strictly into collective funds. Individual bonuses are inappropriate; the organization's collective strength must be prioritized above all.

InstitutionalCollectivism.q: When evaluating a potential new hire, what is the most important factor for you?
options: Their individual track record, unique skills, and personal drive to outperform others.
Their personal achievements, balanced with their ability to work alongside others.
A mix of their individual merit and their potential to fit into the existing team dynamic.
Their willingness to collaborate and their alignment with the organization's collective values.
Their proven ability to work harmoniously within a team and prioritize group goals over personal ambition.
Their background and connections that can benefit the broader organizational community.
Their deep commitment to the collective. Individual brilliance is irrelevant if they do not serve the group's unified purpose.

InstitutionalCollectivism.q: How do you view the role of organizational or societal institutions (like government or corporate leadership) in people's lives?
options: They should interfere as little as possible. Individuals are fully responsible for their own success or failure.
They should provide a basic safety net, but individuals must primarily rely on their own initiative.
They should offer moderate support and regulation to ensure fairness, while preserving individual freedom.
They should play an active role in ensuring resources are distributed fairly and collective well-being is maintained.
They have a strong duty to actively manage resources and protect the collective from individual selfishness.
They must heavily regulate and guide society to ensure absolute collective harmony and resource sharing.
They must strictly enforce collective action and resource distribution. The needs of the society/organization completely override individual desires.

InGroupCollectivism.q: You are offered a prestigious promotion that requires you to relocate, which would mean leaving your close-knit team and family behind. How do you decide?
options: I accept immediately. My individual career advancement is my top priority.
I accept, but I will make sure to visit my family and old team regularly.
I weigh the personal career benefits against the impact on my family, seeking a compromise.
I lean toward declining or negotiating remote work, as my family and current team's stability is highly important to me.
I decline the promotion. My loyalty to my family and my current group outweighs any individual career gain.
I would not even consider it. Uprooting my family or abandoning my group for personal gain is unacceptable.
I outright reject it. My identity and duty are entirely tied to my family and in-group; individual ambition is secondary to their well-being.

InGroupCollectivism.q: A close friend or family member asks you to help them get a job at your company, but they are not the most qualified candidate. What do you do?
options: I refuse. Hiring must be strictly based on merit, and nepotism is unprofessional.
I will review their resume, but I will only recommend them if they are genuinely competitive with other candidates.
I will give their resume a slight boost or an internal referral, but the final decision must be fair.
I will actively advocate for them and highlight their potential, as loyalty to my circle is a key professional value.
I will strongly push for their hiring. Helping my in-group is a moral obligation, even if others are slightly more qualified.
I will use my influence to ensure they get the position. Taking care of my own is more important than abstract corporate meritocracy.
I will do whatever it takes to get them hired. The bond of family/group loyalty supersedes all other professional considerations.

InGroupCollectivism.q: When your organization achieves a major success, how do you prefer to celebrate?
options: By highlighting and rewarding the specific individuals who drove the success.
By acknowledging the key contributors, while noting the team's general support.
By celebrating the team as a whole, while still giving a nod to standout individual efforts.
By focusing entirely on the team's collective effort, avoiding singling out any one person.
By organizing a large group event that reinforces our shared identity and mutual dependence.
By emphasizing that this success belongs to the entire organization/family, with no individual credit taken.
By strictly framing the success as a victory for the collective. Any individual claiming personal credit would be seen as selfish and disruptive.

GenderEgalitarianism.q: Your company is selecting a project manager for a high-stress, high-travel international assignment. Two candidates are equally qualified: one man, one woman. What is your guiding principle?
options: I would subtly favor the male candidate, as men are generally more suited for high-stress, demanding travel roles.
I would lean toward the male candidate, assuming he might have fewer family obligations that could interfere with travel.
I would evaluate them strictly on their individual resumes, but acknowledge that traditional gender roles might make the role slightly harder for the woman.
I would evaluate them completely blindly, ensuring gender plays absolutely zero role in the decision.
I would actively ensure the woman is given equal or preferential consideration to counteract historical biases in such roles.
I would advocate for the woman, believing that breaking traditional gender barriers in high-stress roles is a critical organizational duty.
I would insist on the woman's selection if there is any doubt, as achieving absolute gender parity in leadership is a non-negotiable priority.

GenderEgalitarianism.q: During a meeting, a junior female colleague's idea is talked over by a senior male colleague. How do you react?
options: I do nothing. This is a normal dynamic, and seniority naturally commands the floor.
I feel it's unfortunate, but I assume she will speak up again later if it's truly important.
I might gently steer the conversation back to her if the opportunity arises naturally.
I immediately interject: 'I'd like to hear the rest of what [Name] was saying.'
I actively redirect the conversation to her and explicitly state that her idea is valuable and deserves full attention.
I call out the dynamic directly: 'Let's ensure we are hearing from everyone, regardless of seniority or gender.'
I firmly stop the meeting to address the interruption, making it clear that silencing female colleagues is unacceptable and will be formally addressed.

GenderEgalitarianism.q: How do you view the division of household and professional responsibilities between genders?
options: Men should primarily focus on professional careers, while women should primarily manage the household and family.
Men should be the primary breadwinners, though women can work if they choose, but family remains their main duty.
Both should contribute to work and home, though traditional roles may naturally emerge based on personal preference.
Responsibilities should be divided entirely based on individual skills and agreements, with no regard for gender.
There should be an active, intentional effort to ensure men take on equal shares of domestic and caregiving responsibilities.
Societal and corporate structures must be actively redesigned to eliminate any remaining systemic advantages men have in the workplace.
Gender is entirely irrelevant to capability. Any remaining disparity in roles is a failure of society that must be aggressively corrected.

Assertiveness.q: A business partner proposes a deal that is highly unfavorable to your organization. How do you respond?
options: I firmly and directly reject the proposal, clearly stating why it is unacceptable and outlining my counter-demands.
I push back strongly, pointing out the flaws in their proposal and demanding significant revisions.
I express my concerns clearly but politely, suggesting we work together to find a more balanced middle ground.
I express mild hesitation and suggest we need more time to review, avoiding direct confrontation.
I remain very diplomatic, focusing on our long-term relationship and gently steering the conversation away from the unfavorable terms.
I avoid saying 'no' directly. I use vague language like 'this will be difficult' to signal disagreement without causing offense.
I remain completely silent on the issue during the meeting to preserve harmony, and later use a trusted intermediary to convey my reluctance.

Assertiveness.q: In a team brainstorming session, you strongly disagree with the majority's chosen direction. What do you do?
options: I openly and passionately debate the majority, presenting strong counter-arguments to change their minds.
I voice my disagreement clearly and advocate for my alternative, even if it creates some tension.
I share my alternative perspective respectfully, but I am willing to compromise if the group disagrees.
I keep my disagreement to myself to avoid disrupting the group's momentum and harmony.
I subtly ask questions that might make the group reconsider, without directly stating my own opposition.
I fully support the group's decision outwardly, even though I privately disagree, to maintain team cohesion.
I remain entirely silent. Open disagreement is disrespectful and threatens the harmony of the group.

Assertiveness.q: How do you prefer to handle a situation where a colleague has made a mistake that affects your work?
options: I confront them directly and immediately, demanding they fix it and explaining the negative impact.
I speak to them privately but firmly, making it clear that the mistake is unacceptable and must be corrected.
I discuss it with them constructively, focusing on how we can solve the problem together.
I gently mention the issue and offer to help them fix it, minimizing any sense of blame.
I fix the mistake myself without saying anything, to avoid making them feel embarrassed or defensive.
I ignore the mistake if it's minor, as pointing it out might damage our working relationship.
I would never point out a colleague's mistake directly. Preserving their dignity and our harmony is far more important than the error.

FutureOrientation.q: Your company has a windfall of extra capital. How do you advocate for it to be spent?
options: On immediate bonuses and short-term perks to boost current morale and reward recent efforts.
On quick-win projects that will show a return on investment within the next 6 to 12 months.
On a balanced portfolio: some immediate improvements, and some moderate investment in next year's goals.
Primarily on strategic initiatives that will position the company for growth over the next 3 to 5 years.
Heavily on long-term R&D and infrastructure, even if it means sacrificing short-term profits or bonuses.
Almost entirely on 10-year strategic visions and sustainable legacy projects, with minimal focus on current quarterly results.
Exclusively on generational, long-term investments. Short-term gains are irrelevant compared to securing the organization's distant future.

FutureOrientation.q: You are planning a major career move. What is your primary deciding factor?
options: The immediate salary increase and the perks I can enjoy right now.
The short-term career advancement and the skills I can add to my resume this year.
A balance between a good current role and the potential for moderate growth in the next few years.
The long-term career trajectory and how this move positions me for leadership in 5 years.
The enduring legacy and long-term stability this path provides, even if it requires years of delayed gratification.
How this decision aligns with my 10-to-20 year life vision, prioritizing future security over present comfort.
Entirely on the long-term impact. I am willing to make significant present-day sacrifices to ensure a secure and prosperous distant future.

FutureOrientation.q: How do you view the practice of saving money versus spending it?
options: I prefer to spend on experiences and quality of life now. The future is uncertain, so enjoy the present.
I spend mostly for the present, but I keep a small, basic emergency fund just in case.
I balance enjoying my current income with a disciplined, moderate savings plan for the near future.
I prioritize saving and investing a significant portion of my income to ensure future security and growth.
I aggressively save and invest, often delaying current pleasures to build substantial long-term wealth.
I live very frugally now, channeling almost all resources into long-term investments and future preparations.
I believe in extreme delayed gratification. Present-day spending should be minimized to the absolute essentials to maximize future security.

PerformanceOrientation.q: An employee on your team is a top performer who consistently exceeds targets, but they are arrogant and disrupt team harmony. How do you handle it?
options: I praise and reward them lavishly. Results are all that matter, and harmony is secondary to excellence.
I reward their performance highly, but give them a mild, private warning about their attitude.
I acknowledge their results but have a firm conversation about the need to improve their teamwork and attitude.
I balance my feedback: praising their output while strongly emphasizing that team cohesion is equally important.
I prioritize team harmony. I will formally warn them that their behavior is unacceptable, even if it risks a drop in their output.
I am prepared to let them go if they do not change. A toxic high-performer is more damaging to the organization than a moderate, harmonious one.
I immediately take action to remove or isolate them. Preserving the collective well-being and harmony of the group is absolutely paramount.

PerformanceOrientation.q: When setting annual goals for your department, what is your primary focus?
options: Setting highly aggressive, stretch targets to drive maximum individual competition and excellence.
Setting challenging targets with clear individual rewards for those who outperform their peers.
Setting ambitious but achievable goals, with a mix of individual and team-based incentives.
Setting clear team goals, emphasizing that we succeed or fail together through collaboration.
Setting moderate, realistic goals that prioritize a supportive, low-stress, and harmonious work environment.
Focusing primarily on relationship-building and employee well-being, with performance metrics being a secondary concern.
Avoiding aggressive targets entirely. The primary goal is to maintain a peaceful, conflict-free, and deeply supportive community.

PerformanceOrientation.q: How do you believe a company should recognize and reward success?
options: Through highly visible, individual awards, public recognition, and significant financial bonuses for top achievers.
Through individual merit-based promotions and public acknowledgment of standout contributions.
Through a combination of individual recognition for excellence and team rewards for collaboration.
Through team-based celebrations and shared bonuses that reinforce collective effort.
Through subtle, private acknowledgments that avoid making anyone feel left out or creating unhealthy competition.
By focusing on collective milestones and ensuring that no individual is elevated above the rest of the group.
By avoiding individual competition entirely. Rewards should be distributed equally to maintain perfect harmony and unity.

HumaneOrientation.q: A colleague confides in you that they are going through a severe personal crisis that is affecting their work performance. What is your priority?
options: Their work output. I will politely but firmly remind them of their deadlines and professional responsibilities.
I will express brief sympathy, but I will still expect them to meet their core professional obligations.
I will offer some flexibility and support, but we still need to find a practical solution to keep the project on track.
I will actively help them redistribute their workload and offer significant flexibility, prioritizing their well-being over immediate deadlines.
I will strongly advocate for them to take extended leave, ensuring they have full organizational support, regardless of project delays.
I will personally step in to cover their work and provide emotional support, as their human dignity is far more important than any task.
I will mobilize the entire team to support them unconditionally. The well-being of a person always supersedes any business objective.

HumaneOrientation.q: When evaluating a potential business partner, what trait do you value most?
options: Their efficiency, competence, and ability to deliver results on time and under budget.
Their strong track record of success and their sharp, strategic business acumen.
A balance of their professional competence and their basic decency and fairness.
Their reputation for being fair, trustworthy, and treating their own employees well.
Their demonstrated commitment to social responsibility, kindness, and community support.
Their genuine compassion and altruism. I prefer to work with people who prioritize human welfare over pure profit.
Their deep, proven dedication to philanthropy and helping others. A partner's moral character and generosity are the only true measures of value.

HumaneOrientation.q: How do you view the role of empathy and kindness in a professional workplace?
options: They are largely irrelevant. The workplace is for getting things done efficiently, not for emotional support.
They are nice to have, but professionalism and objectivity must always come first.
They are important, but they should not interfere with making tough, logical business decisions.
They are essential. A good leader or colleague should actively show care and consideration for others' feelings.
They are a core professional value. The workplace should be a supportive, nurturing environment.
They are the foundation of a good workplace. Generosity and compassion should guide most professional interactions.
They are the highest professional ideals. A workplace should function like a caring community, where altruism and mutual support override all else.

CharismaticValueBased.q: Your team is facing a difficult, demoralizing project. How do you motivate them?
options: I focus strictly on the transactional rewards: 'If we finish this, you will get a bonus.'
I outline the practical benefits of completing the project, keeping the focus on the task.
I acknowledge the difficulty but emphasize our shared professional duty to get it done.
I share a compelling vision of how this project will positively impact our clients and our future.
I passionately articulate our core values and inspire them by connecting their daily work to a higher, meaningful purpose.
I lead by personal example, making sacrifices alongside them and using highly inspiring, visionary rhetoric to ignite their passion.
I completely immerse myself in the team's struggle, using profound moral conviction and visionary storytelling to transform their mindset and drive exceptional performance.

CharismaticValueBased.q: When making a major strategic decision, what is your primary guiding principle?
options: Pure data, logic, and immediate financial return.
Practical feasibility and risk management.
A balance of logical analysis and consultation with key stakeholders.
How well the decision aligns with the organization's stated mission and medium-term goals.
How strongly the decision reflects our core, non-negotiable values, even if it is not the easiest path.
I rely heavily on my moral compass and visionary intuition to guide the organization toward a principled future.
I am driven entirely by a deep, unwavering commitment to a higher purpose. The decision must be a testament to our highest ideals, regardless of short-term cost.

CharismaticValueBased.q: How do you handle a situation where the team's performance is slipping?
options: I implement stricter monitoring and tie their pay directly to immediate output.
I set clearer, more specific daily targets and check in frequently.
I hold a meeting to identify practical roadblocks and adjust our workflow.
I remind the team of our shared goals and encourage them to recommit to our standards.
I deliver an inspiring message about our potential, reigniting their belief in our collective mission.
I personally connect with each member, appealing to their sense of pride and our shared values to elevate their effort.
I step in as a visionary catalyst, using powerful, values-driven communication to transform their mindset and inspire them to exceed their own expectations.

TeamOriented.q: Two of your top employees are in a bitter conflict that is disrupting the team. How do you resolve it?
options: I tell them to work it out themselves or I will reassign one of them. I don't have time for drama.
I issue a formal warning that their behavior is affecting productivity and must stop immediately.
I mediate a practical discussion focused on how to divide their tasks to minimize interaction.
I facilitate a meeting to help them understand each other's perspectives and find a professional compromise.
I actively work to rebuild their relationship, emphasizing our shared team goals and the importance of mutual respect.
I invest significant time in team-building and coaching, prioritizing the restoration of group harmony above all immediate project deadlines.
I halt regular work if necessary to facilitate deep, restorative dialogue. The unity and cohesion of the team are the absolute foundation of our success.

TeamOriented.q: When a major project succeeds, how do you handle the recognition?
options: I highlight the specific individuals who did the heavy lifting and ensure they are rewarded.
I acknowledge the key contributors, while mentioning the team's general support.
I celebrate the team's effort, but make sure the project lead gets appropriate individual credit.
I publicly praise the entire team equally, emphasizing that it was a true collaborative effort.
I organize a team-wide celebration and explicitly state that no single person could have achieved this alone.
I deflect all personal credit as a leader and shine the spotlight entirely on the collective effort and shared purpose of the group.
I fiercely protect the narrative that this was purely a collective victory. Individual recognition is secondary to reinforcing the team's unified identity.

TeamOriented.q: How do you prefer to structure your team's workflow?
options: Highly independent. Everyone has their own clear, individual targets and is responsible for their own output.
Mostly independent, with occasional check-ins to ensure individual efforts are loosely aligned.
A mix of individual ownership and collaborative milestones where the group syncs up.
Highly collaborative, with shared goals and regular group problem-solving sessions.
Deeply integrated, where team members constantly support each other and share responsibilities fluidly.
Completely collective. The team functions as a single unit, with shared accountability for every outcome.
Utterly cohesive. Individual roles are blurred in favor of a unified, interdependent group effort where the collective mission is the only focus.

Participative.q: Your organization needs to adopt a new software system. How do you make the decision?
options: I research the options and make the final decision myself to ensure it's done quickly and efficiently.
I make the decision, but I briefly inform the team of my reasoning afterward.
I ask for a few quick opinions from key members, but I retain the final authority to choose.
I hold a meeting to discuss the options, consider the team's feedback, and then make the final call.
I facilitate a collaborative evaluation where the team's consensus heavily dictates the final choice.
I step back and let the team research, debate, and decide together, acting only as a facilitator.
I fully delegate the decision to the team. I believe the best solutions always emerge from collective, democratic deliberation.

Participative.q: A junior team member proposes an idea that contradicts your initial strategy. How do you respond?
options: I politely but firmly dismiss it and reiterate my original strategy.
I acknowledge it, but explain why my strategy is better and move on.
I listen to their idea, but I ultimately steer the conversation back to my original plan.
I genuinely consider their idea, ask questions, and am willing to adjust my strategy if their point is valid.
I actively encourage them to elaborate, and I am highly likely to adopt their idea if it improves our outcome.
I champion their idea to the rest of the group, demonstrating that every voice has the power to shape our direction.
I enthusiastically embrace the challenge to my own strategy. I believe that leaders must constantly be challenged by their team to find the best path forward.

Participative.q: What is your fundamental belief about how decisions should be made in your organization?
options: Decisions should be made swiftly by those at the top who have the clearest view of the big picture.
Leaders should decide, but they have a duty to communicate the 'why' to the team.
Leaders should decide, but they must consult with experts and key stakeholders first.
The best decisions come from a leader who actively listens to and integrates the team's input.
Decision-making should be a shared process, where the leader and the team build the solution together.
The team should have the primary role in decision-making, with the leader acting as a supportive guide.
True innovation and commitment only happen when decisions are made entirely democratically, with maximum participation from everyone affected.

HumaneOriented.q: An employee is consistently missing deadlines due to a difficult personal situation. How do you manage them?
options: I issue a formal performance warning. Personal issues cannot excuse professional failure.
I express sympathy, but I still require them to meet their core deadlines or face consequences.
I offer a slight extension, but I make it clear that this is a one-time exception and performance must improve.
I work with them to temporarily adjust their workload and provide flexible hours to help them cope.
I proactively offer significant support, such as connecting them with HR resources and taking on some of their tasks myself.
I prioritize their well-being entirely, encouraging them to take a leave of absence with full support, regardless of the project's immediate needs.
I treat them with deep compassion and mobilize the entire organization to support them. Their human dignity is infinitely more valuable than any corporate metric.

HumaneOriented.q: How do you define a 'successful' leader?
options: Someone who consistently drives high financial returns and operational efficiency.
Someone who achieves strategic goals while maintaining basic professional standards.
Someone who balances achieving results with treating people fairly and respectfully.
Someone who achieves results while actively fostering a positive, supportive team environment.
Someone who is known for their compassion, generosity, and genuine care for their employees' well-being.
Someone who serves as a mentor and caregiver, prioritizing the personal growth and happiness of their team above all else.
Someone whose legacy is defined entirely by their altruism, selflessness, and the profound, positive impact they have on the lives of others.

HumaneOriented.q: When allocating a limited budget for team improvements, what is your priority?
options: Tools and software that will directly increase productivity and output.
Training programs that will enhance the team's professional skills and performance.
A mix of productivity tools and a modest budget for a team lunch or casual event.
Investing in team-building retreats and resources that improve workplace morale and collaboration.
Funding wellness programs, mental health support, and initiatives that directly improve employees' quality of life.
Direct financial assistance or generous perks for team members who are facing personal or financial hardships.
Channeling resources entirely toward charitable causes or community support, reflecting the team's shared values of generosity and care.

Autonomous.q: You are given a broad, ambiguous mandate to 'improve departmental efficiency.' What is your first move?
options: I immediately consult with my team and stakeholders to gather their ideas and build a consensus on the definition of 'efficiency'.
I hold a series of meetings to understand the current state before proposing any direction.
I gather some data and discuss preliminary ideas with a few trusted colleagues before finalizing a plan.
I analyze the data independently, draft a clear plan, and then present it to the team for feedback.
I rely on my own expertise to quickly design a unique, innovative strategy, and I inform the team of the new direction.
I work entirely independently to craft a bold, unconventional solution, as I trust my own judgment far more than group consensus.
I isolate myself to develop a highly individualistic, disruptive strategy. I believe true innovation requires breaking away from the group's conventional thinking.

Autonomous.q: How do you prefer to manage a highly skilled, experienced team?
options: I facilitate daily collaborative sessions to ensure everyone is perfectly aligned and working together.
I maintain regular, close communication to ensure the team is on track and supporting each other.
I check in weekly to offer guidance, but I expect the team to collaborate and solve most problems together.
I set clear goals and let the team figure out the best way to achieve them together, stepping in only when asked.
I give them broad objectives and trust them to work independently, intervening as little as possible.
I encourage each member to pursue their own unique, independent projects with minimal oversight or group coordination.
I grant them total, unrestricted autonomy. I believe that highly skilled individuals perform best when completely free from collaborative constraints or managerial oversight.

Autonomous.q: When facing a major crisis, what is your leadership instinct?
options: To immediately gather the entire group to brainstorm and decide on a unified response together.
To consult with key advisors quickly, then make a decision that the whole team will execute.
To gather essential input, but take charge of directing the team's coordinated response.
To assess the situation, delegate specific tasks based on expertise, and let the team execute.
To take swift, independent action to stabilize the situation, relying on my own judgment and experience.
To isolate myself, analyze the problem deeply, and craft a unique, independent solution without group input.
To rely entirely on my own individualistic vision. In a crisis, I believe a single, strong, independent mind is far more effective than a committee.

SelfProtective.q: A major project you led has failed publicly, and the media is asking questions. How do you respond?
options: I take full, public responsibility, openly detail my mistakes, and outline how I will personally fix them.
I acknowledge my role in the failure, apologize, and focus on the lessons learned for the future.
I share the responsibility with the team, explaining the complex factors that led to the outcome.
I issue a carefully worded, neutral statement that acknowledges the setback without assigning specific blame.
I emphasize the external factors and market conditions that contributed to the failure, protecting my and the organization's reputation.
I strictly control the narrative, ensuring that the focus remains on the organization's overall strength and my continued competent leadership.
I aggressively defend my track record and the organization's protocols, ensuring that no personal or institutional blame is accepted under any circumstances.

SelfProtective.q: How do you view the use of status symbols (e.g., corner offices, formal titles, exclusive perks) in leadership?
options: They are harmful and create unnecessary barriers. Leaders should sit with the team and reject special treatment.
They are mostly unnecessary. A leader's value comes from their actions, not their title or office.
They are acceptable if they are earned, but they shouldn't be flaunted or used to intimidate.
They are useful tools for establishing clear authority and commanding respect in a professional setting.
They are important for maintaining the dignity of the leadership role and reinforcing the organizational hierarchy.
They are essential. Status symbols protect the leader's authority and ensure that their position is respected and not challenged.
They are absolutely critical. A leader must actively cultivate and display their status and security to maintain control and prevent any threat to their position.

SelfProtective.q: When a new, risky opportunity arises, what is your primary consideration?
options: The potential for massive, disruptive innovation. High risk is worth the reward.
The potential upside, provided we have a basic contingency plan if things go wrong.
A careful calculation of the risk versus reward, ensuring the team is prepared for either outcome.
How this opportunity might impact the team's stability, and ensuring we have strong safeguards in place.
How this decision will reflect on my leadership and the organization's reputation. I must avoid any move that could be seen as reckless.
I prioritize protecting my position and the organization's current standing. I will only proceed if the risk to my authority is virtually zero.
I will likely reject it. My primary duty is to ensure absolute security, stability, and the preservation of the status quo to protect my leadership position.
